title: A Daily Pill Just Doubled Survival for Pancreatic Cancer. For Diabetes-Prone South Asians, the Breakthrough Hits Close to Home.
excerpt: Daraxonrasib, the first RAS inhibitor, cut the risk of death by 60 per cent in a 500-patient trial — the largest gain ever recorded for advanced pancreatic cancer.
body:
Pancreatic cancer has long been medicine's cruellest dead end. Diagnosed late, resistant to treatment, and almost universally fatal once it spreads, it kills roughly 53,000 Americans every year with a five-year survival rate that hovers around three per cent for metastatic cases. For patients who fail their first round of chemotherapy, the options have historically ranged from bad to worse.

That changed on Sunday at the American Society of Clinical Oncology's annual meeting in Chicago, where researchers presented full results from a 500-person trial showing that a once-daily pill called daraxonrasib doubled survival compared with standard chemotherapy — and did it with fewer severe side effects.

## A Drug That Ticks Every Box

Patients taking daraxonrasib lived a median of 13.2 months, compared with 6.7 months for those on chemotherapy. The drug cut the overall risk of death by 60 per cent. In patients with a specific RAS mutation known as G12 — present in over 90 per cent of pancreatic cancers — tumours remained under control for 7.3 months versus 3.5 months on chemo.

"It ticks all of the boxes," said Dr. Rachna Shroff of the University of Arizona Cancer Center. "A doubling of survival and reduction in the risk of death has never been seen in patients whose cancer progressed after chemotherapy."

Dr. Julie Gralow, chief medical officer of ASCO, called it a "grand slam" — a phrase seldom used at oncology conferences, where incremental progress is the norm.

## The Indian Connection

The trial's co-principal investigator is Dr. Shubham Pant, a surgical oncologist at the University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center and one of the most prominent Indian-origin researchers in pancreatic cancer. Dr. Pant described patients who had abandoned daily activities resuming them within weeks of starting the drug.

"I have multiple patients like that," he said, citing one avid golfer who reduced his reliance on narcotics and returned to the course after a month on treatment.

The lead principal investigator, Dr. Brian Wolpin of Harvard's Dana-Farber Cancer Institute, said the results "will change how scientists, clinicians, and patients think about treatment for pancreatic cancer."

## Why South Asians Should Pay Attention

Pancreatic cancer disproportionately affects people with Type 2 diabetes — a condition that runs at epidemic levels in the South Asian community. Studies show that South Asians with longstanding diabetes have a two to threefold higher risk of developing pancreatic cancer. The diaspora's genetic predisposition to insulin resistance makes early screening and awareness even more critical.

Daraxonrasib is the first in a new class of drugs called RAS(ON) inhibitors, which target the mutant RAS protein that fuels tumour growth. The FDA granted expanded access to the drug on May 1 and plans an accelerated review. Revolution Medicines, the drug's manufacturer, is already testing it in earlier-stage disease and in combination with other treatments.

## The Rash Question

The main concern remains rash, experienced by 86.3 per cent of patients. But severe rash occurred in only 14 per cent of cases, and critically, just 1.2 per cent of patients on daraxonrasib dropped out due to side effects — compared with 11.2 per cent of those on chemotherapy. Most rashes were manageable with antibiotics and topical steroids.

Severe side effects overall were lower on the drug (43.6 per cent) than on chemotherapy (57.5 per cent).

## What Comes Next

Menta "Steve" Wallace, a 74-year-old from Houston, is in one of the follow-up trials testing daraxonrasib as a first-line treatment. His tumour has shrunk by 46 per cent in four months. He is planning a Caribbean cruise at the end of June — packing his pills on ice.

For the thousands of South Asian families who have watched loved ones disappear into the black hole of a pancreatic cancer diagnosis, this is the first real reason for hope in a generation.
